newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan keeps low-profile on U.S. missile contract.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan keeps low-profile on U.S. missile contract.

text.p: Taiwan's military kept a low-profile on Tuesday after the U.S. army awarded a missile contract and Taipei's silence is seen as an attempt to prevent feared protests from rival China.

The Army announced without elaboration that it had awarded the US$63 million contract to Boeing Defence and Space Group, Missiles and Space Division, in Huntsville, Alabama, to produce 74 Avenger fire units for Taiwan.
Taiwan's military spokesman declined to comment.
"It is inappropriate to discuss any aspects of military deployment, such as the use of military personnel or artillery," spokesman Kung Fan-ting told reporters when asked about the missile contract.
The Army's announcement came just days before a relations-mending trip to Washington by a delegation headed by Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian.
The Avenger is a mobile anti-aircraft defence missile system that can launch eight Stinger missiles from two reloadable pods.
Taiwan also planned to buy 68 batteries of French Mistral missiles, but the deal has not yet finalised, state-funded television reported.
The U.S. Defence Department approved the Taiwan sale last summer despite a warning from China's Foreign Ministry that it would cause "new damage" to improving U.S.-China relations.
General Chi and a 20-member senior delegation from China's defence and foreign ministries is to arrive on Thursday for a two-week visit at the invitation of Defence Secretary William Perry.
Taiwan and China have been rivals since the Nationalist government lost the Chinese civil war to the communists and fled into exile to Taiwan in 1949.
Since then, Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province not entitled to foreign ties and vows to retake the island by force if Taipei opts for independence.
Despite switching diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979, Washington reserves the right to provide Taiwan with defensive weapons.
China strongly objects to military links between the island and foreign countries.
Earlier this year, Beijing carried out a series of war games in waters off Taiwan intended to intimidate voters in the run-up to Taiwan's first-ever direct presidential election.
